segments.text: A small jet hits a jungle mountain in a storm. Thirty-one people on board. One of them wakes up in the wreck, under a seat, with her jaw broken and one lung collapsed.
Hurt like that, alone up there? No chance. Let's go back to the start.
Annette Herfkens is Dutch, a trader at a bank in Madrid. Her fiancé, Willem van der Pas, works for a bank in Vietnam. She calls him Pasje. They've been together thirteen years.
November {1992|nineteen ninety-two}. She flies out to see him, and he has planned a few days by the sea, in Nha Trang.
But the plane is small, and she's claustrophobic. She doesn't want to get on. He tells her it's only twenty minutes.
It isn't. Well into the flight, the plane drops. He looks at her, frightened. An air pocket, she tells him. Then it drops again. He grabs her hand. And everything goes black.
In bad weather, the jet had come down too low, and hit the trees on a ridge. She wasn't wearing a seat belt. She wakes with a seat on top of her.
Willem is still in his seat. He is dead. She has said there was a smile on his face.
One other passenger is alive: a Vietnamese businessman. Her skirt is gone, so he gives her a pair of trousers from his suitcase. He tells her rescuers will come. Before long, he dies too.
Now she's alone on a mountain. Her hip is shattered. And she has no water.
So she decides to stay put and wait. And she refuses to think about Pasje. Crying would only make her weaker.
Then she sees the broken wing. Its insulation is soft, like a sponge. I squeezed it myself. She drags herself to it on her elbows, pulls out tufts, and rolls them into balls.
When rain comes, they soak it up. She allows herself one sip every two hours. Rainwater is all she has.
The jungle moves in. Leeches. Insects. And the smell of the wreck. She drags herself away from it.
And nobody comes. The wreck lies on a mountain called O Kha, and day after day, nobody finds it.
So she stays in the moment, she has said, and finds her calm in the beauty of the jungle.
After nearly a week, she feels herself slipping away. She has described that feeling as beautiful.
Then a man in orange appears among the trees. He looks at her. And he goes away again.
On day eight, men climb up to the wreck: a police officer, who she has said took her for a ghost, and others carrying body bags and a passenger list. She points to her own name.
They carry her down the mountain in a sling of canvas. She is taken to hospital, in Singapore.
Back home, her family already believed she was dead. Death notices had been published. One colleague, Jaime Lupa, had refused to believe it.
In December, in the Dutch town of Breda, she goes to Willem's funeral, on a stretcher. She has compared it to a bride being taken down the aisle, to meet her groom.
By New Year's Eve she is walking. By February she's back at work.
She marries Jaime, moves to New York, and raises two children, Joosje and Max. In {2006|two thousand and six} she goes back to that mountain. And she writes it all down, in a book called Turbulence.
Thirty people died on that ridge. A helicopter sent out for the wreck crashed too, and more lives were lost.
One person lived. Eight days, on rainwater, and one rule: stay in the moment. I said no chance. I was wrong. Case closed.
